L1142: ## API overview
L1143:   * `thread/start` - create a new thread; emits `thread/started` and automatically subscribes you to turn/item events for that thread.
L1144:   * `thread/resume` - reopen an existing thread by id so later `turn/start` calls append to it.
L1145:   * `thread/fork` - fork a thread into a new thread id by copying stored history. Pass `lastTurnId` to copy history through that turn and omit later turns, or `ephemeral: true` to create an in-memory fork. Emits `thread/started` for the new thread; returned threads include `forkedFromId` when available.
L1146:   * `thread/read` - read a stored thread by id without resuming it; set `includeTurns` to return full turn history. Returned `thread` objects include runtime `status`.
L1147:   * `thread/list` - page through stored thread logs; supports cursor-based pagination plus `modelProviders`, `sourceKinds`, `archived`, `isPinned`, `cwd`, `useStateDbOnly`, `searchTerm`, and experimental `parentThreadId` or `ancestorThreadId` filters. Returned `thread` objects include runtime `status`.
L1148:   * `thread/turns/list` - experimental; page through a stored thread’s turn history without resuming it. `itemsView` controls whether turn items are omitted, summarized, or fully loaded.
L1149:   * `thread/items/list` - experimental; page through persisted thread items, optionally restricted to one `turnId`. The active thread store must support item pagination.
L1150:   * `thread/loaded/list` - list the thread ids currently loaded in memory.
L1151:   * `thread/name/set` - set or update a thread’s user-facing name for a loaded thread or a persisted rollout; emits `thread/name/updated`.
L1152:   * `thread/goal/set` - set the goal for a thread; emits `thread/goal/updated`.
L1153:   * `thread/goal/get` - read the current goal for a thread.
L1154:   * `thread/goal/clear` - clear the goal for a thread; emits `thread/goal/cleared`.
L1155:   * `thread/metadata/update` - patch SQLite-backed stored thread metadata, including persisted `gitInfo` and `isPinned`.
L1156:   * `thread/archive` - move a thread’s log file into the archived directory and attempt to archive spawned descendant thread logs that aren’t already archived; returns `{}` on success and emits `thread/archived` for each archived thread.
L1157:   * `thread/delete` - permanently delete a persisted active or archived thread and any spawned descendant threads; returns `{}` on success and emits `thread/deleted` for each deleted thread.
L1158:   * `thread/unsubscribe` - unsubscribe this connection from thread turn/item events. If this was the last subscriber, the server unloads the thread after a no-subscriber inactivity grace period and emits `thread/closed`.
L1159:   * `thread/unarchive` - restore an archived thread rollout back into the active sessions directory; returns the restored `thread` and emits `thread/unarchived`.
L1160:   * `thread/status/changed` - notification emitted when a loaded thread’s runtime `status` changes.
L1161:   * `thread/compact/start` - trigger conversation history compaction for a thread; returns `{}` immediately while progress streams via `turn/*` and `item/*` notifications.
L1162:   * `thread/shellCommand` - run a user-initiated shell command against a thread. This runs outside the sandbox with full access and doesn’t inherit the thread sandbox policy.

L964: ## Create a skill
L965: 
L966: If you already know the workflow and it’s easier to show than describe, use cite364†Record & Replay . The recorder captures the workflow, inspects the steps, and drafts a reusable skill from the demonstration.
L967: 
L968: If you want to describe the skill instead, use the built-in creator. In ChatGPT Work, invoke it as `@skill-creator`. In Codex, invoke it as:
L969: 
L970:     `$skill-creator`
L971: The creator asks what the skill does, when it should trigger, and whether it should stay instruction-only or include scripts. Instruction-only is the default.
L972: 
L973: You can also create a skill manually by creating a folder with a `SKILL.md` file:
L974: 
L975:     `---
L976:     name: skill-name
L977:     description: Explain exactly when this skill should and should not trigger.
L978:     ---
L979: 
L980:     Skill instructions for ChatGPT or Codex to follow.`
L981: Codex detects skill changes automatically. If an update doesn’t appear, restart Codex.
L982: ## Where Codex loads local skills
L983: 
L984: Codex reads skills from repository, user, admin, and system locations. For repositories, Codex scans `.agents/skills` in every directory from your current working directory up to the repository root. If two skills share the same `name`, Codex doesn’t merge them; both can appear in skill selectors.
L985: Skill Scope  | Location  | Suggested use
L986: --- | --- | ---
L987: `REPO`  | `$CWD/.agents/skills`
L988: Current working directory: where you launch Codex.  | If you’re in a repository or code environment, teams can check in skills relevant to a working folder. For example, skills only relevant to a microservice or a module.
L989: `REPO`  | `$CWD/../.agents/skills`
L990: A folder above CWD when you launch Codex inside a Git repository.  | If you’re in a repository with nested folders, organizations can check in skills relevant to a shared area in a parent folder.
L991: `REPO`  | `$REPO_ROOT/.agents/skills`
L992: The topmost root folder when you launch Codex inside a Git repository.  | If you’re in a repository with nested folders, organizations can check in skills relevant to everyone using the repository. These serve as root skills available to any subfolder in the repository.
L993: `USER`  | `$HOME/.agents/skills`
L994: Any skills checked into the user’s personal folder.  | Use to curate skills relevant to a user that apply to any repository the user may work in.
L995: `ADMIN`  | `/etc/codex/skills`
L996: Any skills checked into the machine or container in a shared, system location.  | Use for SDK scripts, automation, and for checking in default admin skills available to each user on the machine.
L997: `SYSTEM`  | Bundled with Codex by OpenAI.  | Useful skills relevant to a broad audience such as the skill-creator and plan skills. Available to everyone when they start Codex.
L998: Codex supports symlinked skill folders and follows the symlink target when scanning these locations.
L999: 
L1000: These locations are for authoring and local discovery. When you want to distribute reusable skills beyond a single repo, or optionally bundle them with connectors, use cite526†plugins†developers.openai.com .
L1001: ## Distribute skills with plugins
L1002: 
L1003: Direct skill folders are best for local authoring and repo-scoped workflows. If you want to distribute a reusable skill, bundle two or more skills together, or ship a skill alongside a connector, package them as a cite526†plugin†developers.openai.com .
L1004: 
L1005: Plugins can include one or more skills. They can also optionally bundle registered MCP server connections, bundled MCP server configuration, and presentation assets in a single package.
L1006: ## Install curated skills for local use
L1007: 
L1008: To add curated skills beyond the built-ins for your own local Codex setup, use `$skill-installer`. For example, to install the `$linear` skill:
L1009: 
L1010:     `$skill-installer linear`
L1011: 
L1012: You can also prompt the installer to download skills from other repositories. Codex detects newly installed skills automatically; if one doesn’t appear, restart Codex.
L1013: 
L1014: Use this for local setup and experimentation. For reusable distribution of your own skills, prefer plugins.
L1015: ## Enable or disable local Codex skills
L1016: 
L1017: Use `[[skills.config]]` entries in `~/.codex/config.toml` to disable a skill without deleting it:
L1018: 
L1019:     `[[skills.config]]
L1020:     path = "/path/to/skill/SKILL.md"
L1021:     enabled = false`
L1022: 
L1023: Restart Codex after changing `~/.codex/config.toml`.
L1024: ## Optional metadata
L1025: Add `agents/openai.yaml` to configure UI metadata in the cite309†ChatGPT desktop app , to set invocation policy, and to declare tool dependencies for a more seamless experience with using the skill.
L1026: 
L1027:     `interface:
L1028:       display_name: "Optional user-facing name"
L1029:       short_description: "Optional user-facing description"
L1030:       icon_small: "./assets/small-logo.svg"
L1031:       icon_large: "./assets/large-logo.png"
L1032:       brand_color: "#3B82F6"
L1033:       default_prompt: "Optional surrounding prompt to use the skill with"
L1034: 
L1035:     policy:
L1036:       allow_implicit_invocation: false
L1037: 
L1038:     dependencies:
L1039:       tools:
L1040:         - type: "mcp"
L1041:           value: "openaiDeveloperDocs"
L1042:           description: "OpenAI Docs MCP server"
L1043:           transport: "streamable_http"
L1044:           url: "https://developers.openai.com/mcp"`
L1045: `allow_implicit_invocation` (default: `true`): When `false`, Codex won’t implicitly invoke the skill based on user prompt; explicit `$skill` invocation still works.
L1046: ## Best practices
L1047: 
L1048:   * Keep each skill focused on one job.
L1049:   * Prefer instructions over scripts unless you need deterministic behavior or external tooling.
L1050:   * Write imperative steps with explicit inputs and outputs.
L1051:   * Test prompts against the skill description to confirm the right trigger behavior.

L947: ## Triggering subagent workflows
L948: 
L949: At most intelligence levels, ask for subagents or parallel agent work directly. Ultra enables proactive delegation, so ChatGPT can delegate suitable independent work without a separate request.
L950: 
L951: Ask for subagents or parallel agent work directly. Codex can also delegate when applicable project or skill instructions request it.
L952: In practice, manual triggering means using direct instructions such as “spawn two agents,” “delegate this work in parallel,” or “use one agent per point.” Subagent workflows consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs because each subagent does its own model and tool work.
L953: A good subagent prompt should explain how to divide the work, whether Codex should wait for all agents before continuing, and what summary or output to return.
L954: 
L955:     `Review this branch with parallel subagents. Spawn one subagent for security risks, one for test gaps, and one for maintainability. Wait for all three, then summarize the findings by category with file references.`
L956: ## Choosing models and reasoning
L957: 
L958: Different agents need different model and reasoning settings.
L959: 
L960: In ChatGPT Work, choose a model and an intelligence level from the composer. Available intelligence levels can include Light, Medium, High, Extra High, and Max, depending on the selected model. Ultra is available only to eligible accounts and supported models. It uses maximum reasoning and lets ChatGPT proactively delegate suitable work to subagents.
L961: At other intelligence levels, ask for subagents explicitly when you want work delegated in parallel.
L962: If you don’t configure a subagent model or `model_reasoning_effort`, the subagent inherits the parent agent’s model and reasoning effort. If an explicit spawn request or an `[agents]` default selects a model without an explicit or configured reasoning effort, the subagent uses that model’s default reasoning effort.
L963: To balance intelligence, speed, and price for each task, request a specific model or reasoning effort in your prompt, configure `[agents]` defaults in `config.toml`, or set `model` and `model_reasoning_effort` directly in the custom agent file. For example, use `gpt-6-luna` for fast scans or a higher-effort `gpt-6.1-sol` configuration for more demanding reasoning.
L964: For most tasks in Codex, start with `gpt-6.1-sol` when your signed-in account or workspace has cite527†access . Otherwise, choose a model available to you. Use `gpt-6-luna` when you want a faster, lower-cost option for lighter subagent work.
L965: ### Model choice
L966: 
L967:   * `gpt-6.1-sol`: Start here for demanding agents. Use it for ambiguous, multi-step work that needs planning, tool use, validation, and follow-through across a larger context.
L968:   * `gpt-6-luna`: Use for fast, narrowly scoped agents handling clear, repeatable, or high-volume work.
L969: ### Reasoning effort (`model_reasoning_effort`)
L970: 
L971: For GPT-6.1 Sol, use a reasoning effort supported by your client and selected model. For explicit model settings, start with `high` for GPT-6 Luna or `low` for GPT-6 Astra. Adjust for the task using a level the selected model supports.
L972:   * `ultra`: Use for the deepest reasoning when the selected model supports it.
L973:   * `max` and `xhigh`: Use for especially demanding reasoning when the selected model supports these levels.
L974:   * `high`: Use when an agent needs to trace complex logic, check assumptions, or work through edge cases (for example, reviewer or security-focused agents).
L975:   * `medium`: Balances speed and depth.
L976:   * `low`: Use when the task is straightforward and speed matters most.
L977: Higher reasoning effort increases response time and token usage, but it can improve quality for complex work. For details, see cite306†Models , cite355†Config basics , and cite357†Configuration Reference .
L978: ## Orchestration and thread controls
L979: 
L980: ChatGPT or Codex handles orchestration across agents, including spawning new subagents, routing follow-up instructions, waiting for results, and closing agent threads.
L981: 
L982: When many agents are running, Codex waits until all requested results are available, then returns a consolidated response.
L983: 
L984: At most intelligence levels, ChatGPT spawns agents after a direct request. With Ultra, ChatGPT can also delegate proactively when parallel work is useful.
L985: Current local Codex releases spawn agents after a direct request or applicable project or skill instruction.
L986: 
L987: To see it in action, try the following prompt on your project:
L988: 
L989:     `I would like to review the following points on the current PR (this branch vs main). Spawn one agent per point, wait for all of them, and summarize the result for each point.
L990:     1. Security issue
L991:     2. Code quality
L992:     3. Bugs
L993:     4. Race
L994:     5. Test flakiness
L995:     6. Maintainability of the code`

L1030: ## Approvals and sandbox controls
L1031: 
L1032: Subagents inherit your current sandbox policy.
L1033: 
L1034: ChatGPT Work runs subagents in its hosted environment and doesn’t expose a local Codex sandbox or approval-mode control. Subagents use the tools available to the parent chat. Website and connector permissions remain tool-specific.
L1035: 
L1036: Subagents inherit the permission mode selected beneath the composer. Choose the permission mode for the parent turn before you ask Codex to delegate work.
L1037: In interactive CLI sessions, approval requests can surface from inactive agent threads even while you are looking at the main thread. The approval overlay shows the source thread label, and you can press `o` to open that thread before you approve, reject, or answer the request.
L1038: 
L1039: In non-interactive flows, or whenever a run can’t surface a fresh approval, an action that needs new approval fails and Codex surfaces the error back to the parent workflow.
L1040: Codex also reapplies the parent turn’s live runtime overrides when it spawns a child. That includes sandbox and approval choices you set interactively during the session, such as `/permissions` changes or `--yolo`, even if the selected custom agent file sets different defaults.
L1041: 
L1042: Subagents inherit the permission mode selected beneath the composer. Choose the permission mode for the parent turn before you ask Codex to delegate work.
L1043: You can also override the sandbox configuration for individual cite531†custom agents , such as explicitly marking one to work in read-only mode.
L1044: ## Custom agents
L1045: 
L1046: Codex ships with built-in agents:
L1047: 
L1048:   * `default`: general-purpose fallback agent.
L1049:   * `worker`: execution-focused agent for implementation and fixes.
L1050:   * `explorer`: read-heavy codebase exploration agent.
L1051: 
L1052: To define your own custom agents, add standalone TOML files under `~/.codex/agents/` for personal agents or `.codex/agents/` for project-scoped agents.
L1053: Each file defines one custom agent. Codex loads these files as configuration layers for spawned sessions, so custom agents can override the same settings as a normal Codex session config. That can feel heavier than a dedicated agent manifest, and the format may evolve as authoring and sharing mature.
L1054: 
L1055: Every standalone custom agent file must define:
L1056: 
L1057:   * `name`
L1058:   * `description`
L1059:   * `developer_instructions`
L1060: If a custom agent file sets `model` or `model_reasoning_effort`, the value in the file takes precedence. Before applying the file, Codex resolves each setting from an explicit spawn value, then the corresponding `[agents]` default, then the parent’s value. If an explicit spawn request or an `[agents]` default selects a model and neither supplies a reasoning effort, Codex uses that model’s default effort. A custom agent file that sets only `model` preserves this previously resolved effort.
L1061: Set `model_reasoning_effort` in the file too if the selected model doesn’t support that effort or you want a different one. Other session settings, such as `sandbox_mode`, `mcp_servers`, and `skills.config`, inherit from the parent when the custom agent file omits them.
L1062: ### Global settings
L1063: 
L1064: Global subagent settings still live under `[agents]` in your cite532†configuration .
L1065: Field  | Type  | Required  | Purpose
L1066: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1067: `agents.enabled`  | boolean  | No  | Enable or disable multi-agent tools.
L1068: `agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session`  | number  | No  | Cap concurrently open spawned-agent threads, excluding the primary.
L1069: `agents.default_subagent_model`  | string  | No  | Set the default model for spawned agents.
L1070: `agents.default_subagent_reasoning_effort`  | string  | No  | Set the default reasoning effort for spawned agents.
L1071: `agents.interrupt_message`  | boolean  | No  | Record a model-visible message when an agent turn is interrupted.
L1072: Notes:
L1073:   * `agents.enabled` defaults to `true`. Set it to `false` to disable multi-agent tools.
L1074:   * When you leave `agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session` unset, Codex chooses the default. Existing configurations can keep using `agents.max_threads` as a legacy alias.
L1075:   * Explicit spawn values override `agents.default_subagent_model` and `agents.default_subagent_reasoning_effort`.
L1076:   * `agents.interrupt_message` defaults to `true`. Set it to `false` to omit the model-visible interruption message from the agent’s context.
L1077:   * If a custom agent name matches a built-in agent such as `explorer`, your custom agent takes precedence.
L1078: ### Custom agent file schema
L1079: 
L1080: Field  | Type  | Required  | Purpose
L1081: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1082: `name`  | string  | Yes  | Agent name Codex uses when spawning or referring to this agent.
L1083: `description`  | string  | Yes  | Human-facing guidance for when Codex should use this agent.
L1084: `developer_instructions`  | string  | Yes  | Core instructions that define the agent’s behavior.
L1085: You can also include other supported `config.toml` keys in a custom agent file, such as `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, `sandbox_mode`, `mcp_servers`, and `skills.config`.
L1086: 
L1087: Codex identifies the custom agent by its `name` field. Matching the filename to the agent name is the simplest convention, but the `name` field is the source of truth.
L1088: ### Example custom agents
L1089: 
L1090: The best custom agents are narrow and opinionated. Give each one clear job, a tool surface that matches that job, and instructions that keep it from drifting into adjacent work.
L1091: 
L1092: The examples use cite527†GPT-6.1 Sol where your signed-in account or workspace has access. If it isn’t available, choose a model you can use.
L1093: #### Example 1: PR review
L1094: 
L1095: This pattern splits review across three focused custom agents:
L1096: 
L1097:   * `pr_explorer` maps the codebase and gathers evidence.
L1098:   * `reviewer` looks for correctness, security, and test risks.
L1099:   * `docs_researcher` checks framework or API documentation through a dedicated MCP server.
L1100: 
L1101: Project config (`.codex/config.toml`):
L1102: 
L1103:     `[agents]
L1104:     max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 8`
